[2024 summer phd math-stat — problem 3]

Part I, Problem 3 (Inference in High-dimensional Regression). Consider $y_i = X_{i\cdot}^\top \beta + \varepsilon_i$, $1 \le i \le n$, with $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p$, $\|\beta\|_0 \le k$, $\varepsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$.
1. Define the Lasso estimator $\hat\beta$ and discuss the challenge of statistical inference with it.
2. Write one form of the debiased Lasso estimator for $\beta_j$ ($1 \le j \le p$) and establish its limiting distribution.
3. Construct a confidence interval for $\beta_j$, estimating $\sigma^2$ in a data-dependent way.

response.text:
## 1. Lasso and the inference difficulty

Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have rows \(X_{i\cdot}^\top\), and write

\[
y=X\beta+\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n).
\]

Assume the columns of \(X\) are standardized, e.g. \(\|X_j\|_2^2/n=1\). The Lasso estimator is

\[
\widehat\beta
\in
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda\|b\|_1
\right\},
\]

with tuning parameter typically \(\lambda\asymp \sigma\sqrt{\log p/n}\).

The main inference difficulty is that the Lasso is biased because of the \(\ell_1\)-penalty. Even in the orthogonal case \(X^\top X/n=I_p\), the Lasso is a coordinatewise soft-thresholding estimator,

\[
\widehat\beta_j
=
\operatorname{sgn}(z_j)(|z_j|-\lambda)_+,
\qquad 
z_j=\beta_j+\frac{X_j^\top\varepsilon}{n},
\]

so its distribution is non-Gaussian and has a point mass at \(0\). Thus naive Wald-type intervals centered at \(\widehat\beta_j\) are invalid. In high dimension \(p\gg n\), ordinary least squares is unavailable because \(X^\top X\) is singular, and post-selection inference after choosing a model by Lasso is also nonstandard because the selected model is random. The debiased Lasso corrects the first-order shrinkage bias.

---

## 2. Debiased Lasso and limiting distribution

Let

\[
\widehat\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}X^\top X.
\]

We want a vector \(\widehat\theta_j\in\mathbb R^p\) such that

\[
\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j \approx e_j,
\]

where \(e_j\) is the \(j\)th standard basis vector. One common construction is the nodewise Lasso.

For fixed \(j\), regress \(X_j\) on \(X_{-j}\):

\[
\widehat\gamma_j
\in
\arg\min_{\gamma\in\mathbb R^{p-1}}
\left\{
\frac{1}{2n}\|X_j-X_{-j}\gamma\|_2^2+\lambda_j\|\gamma\|_1
\right\},
\qquad 
\lambda_j\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

Let

\[
\widehat r_j=X_j-X_{-j}\widehat\gamma_j,
\]

and define \(\widehat c_j\in\mathbb R^p\) by

\[
(\widehat c_j)_j=1,
\qquad
(\widehat c_j)_\ell=-(\widehat\gamma_j)_\ell,\quad \ell\neq j.
\]

Then \(X\widehat c_j=\widehat r_j\). Define

\[
\widehat\tau_j^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|\widehat r_j\|_2^2+\lambda_j\|\widehat\gamma_j\|_1,
\qquad
\widehat\theta_j
=
\frac{\widehat c_j}{\widehat\tau_j^2}.
\]

By the KKT conditions for the nodewise Lasso,

\[
\|\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
\lesssim \lambda_j
\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

The debiased Lasso estimator of \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\widetilde\beta_j
=
\widehat\beta_j
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top(y-X\widehat\beta).
\]

Using \(y=X\beta+\varepsilon\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
&=
\widehat\beta_j-\beta_j
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top X(\beta-\widehat\beta)
+
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon \\
&=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon
+
(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus

\[
\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j
=
\underbrace{\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon}_{\text{Gaussian leading term}}
+
\underbrace{(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)}_{\text{remainder}}.
\]

Assume the usual high-dimensional conditions: a restricted eigenvalue or compatibility condition for \(X\), sparsity \(\|\beta\|_0\le k\), and

\[
k\frac{\log p}{\sqrt n}\to 0.
\]

Then by the standard Lasso oracle inequality,

\[
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\left(k\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}\right).
\]

Therefore the remainder satisfies

\[
\left|
(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)
\right|
\le
\|\widehat\Sigma\widehat\theta_j-e_j\|_\infty
\|\widehat\beta-\beta\|_1
=
O_p\left(\sigma k\frac{\log p}{n}\right),
\]

so

\[
\sqrt n\,
(e_j-\widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta)
=
o_p(\sigma).
\]

Let

\[
\widehat V_j
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j.
\]

Conditional on \(X\),

\[
\widehat\theta_j^\top \frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon
\sim
N\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\widehat V_j\right),
\]

because \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)\). Hence

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)}
{\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
=
\frac{
\widehat\theta_j^\top X^\top\varepsilon
}{
\sigma\sqrt{n\widehat V_j}
}
+
o_p(1)
\;\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\;
N(0,1).
\]

Equivalently, if \(\widehat V_j\to_p V_j\), then

\[
\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N(0,\sigma^2 V_j).
\]

In the common random-design setting with \(\Sigma=\mathbb E[X_iX_i^\top]\) and precision matrix \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\), one typically has \(V_j=\Theta_{jj}\), so

\[
\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N(0,\sigma^2\Theta_{jj}).
\]

---

## 3. Confidence interval with data-dependent variance estimation

We need estimate \(\sigma^2\). A convenient fully data-dependent method is the square-root/scaled Lasso:

\[
(\widehat\beta^{\,0},\widehat\sigma)
\in
\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p,\ \tau>0}
\left\{
\frac{\|y-Xb\|_2^2}{2n\tau}
+\frac{\tau}{2}
+\lambda_0\|b\|_1
\right\},
\qquad 
\lambda_0\asymp \sqrt{\frac{\log p}{n}}.
\]

For fixed \(b\), the minimizing \(\tau\) is

\[
\tau=\frac{\|y-Xb\|_2}{\sqrt n},
\]

so \(\widehat\sigma\) is essentially the residual scale estimate. Under the same restricted eigenvalue and sparsity assumptions,

\[
\widehat\sigma/\sigma \xrightarrow{p} 1.
\]

Alternatively, one may take the residual variance estimator

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|y-X\widehat\beta\|_2^2.
\]

Indeed, writing \(\Delta=\widehat\beta-\beta\),

\[
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|\varepsilon-X\Delta\|_2^2
=
\frac{1}{n}\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
+
\frac{1}{n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
-
\frac{2}{n}\varepsilon^\top X\Delta.
\]

By the Lasso prediction bound,

\[
\frac{1}{n}\|X\Delta\|_2^2
=
O_p\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right)
=
o_p(\sigma^2),
\]

and

\[
\left|
\frac{1}{n}\varepsilon^\top X\Delta
\right|
\le
\left\|\frac{1}{n}X^\top\varepsilon\right\|_\infty
\|\Delta\|_1
=
O_p\left(\sigma^2 k\frac{\log p}{n}\right)
=
o_p(\sigma^2).
\]

Also,

\[
\frac{1}{n}\|\varepsilon\|_2^2
\xrightarrow{p}
\sigma^2
\]

by the law of large numbers. Hence \(\widehat\sigma^2\to_p\sigma^2\).

Therefore an asymptotic \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is

\[
\boxed{
\mathrm{CI}_{j,1-\alpha}
=
\left[
\widetilde\beta_j
-
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}},
\;
\widetilde\beta_j
+
z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat\sigma
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat V_j}{n}}
\right],
}
\]

where

\[
\widehat V_j
=
\widehat\theta_j^\top \widehat\Sigma \widehat\theta_j.
\]

By Slutsky’s theorem,

\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\widetilde\beta_j-\beta_j)}
{\widehat\sigma\sqrt{\widehat V_j}}
\xrightarrow{d}
N(0,1),
\]

so

\[
\mathbb P\left(\beta_j\in \mathrm{CI}_{j,1-\alpha}\right)
\to
1-\alpha.
\]

Thus the debiased Lasso yields asymptotically valid coordinatewise inference despite \(p\) possibly being much larger than \(n\).
